title: the Shiva Purana (selections)
hook: the creator's world won't grow, and the answer appears in a single figure: half Shiva, half the goddess

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Shiva Purana, three cities lined up and fell to one arrow, and the whole world was Shiva's chariot. What did you do with everything lined up behind it? Today, the last selection. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.
screen: `WHEN EVERYTHING LINES UP, ONE ACT GOES THROUGH.` · `THE LAST SELECTION.`

segments.voice: A bronze figure stands with a slight sway at the hip. Look at its right side: a man's flat chest, matted hair piled high, a snake for an earring. Now the left side: a woman's breast, smooth braided hair, a round earring, an anklet on the foot, the hip curving out. Not two figures standing close. One figure, split down the middle. This is Ardhanarishvara, and the Shiva Purana tells a story about why the creator needed to see it.
screen: `RIGHT SIDE: MATTED HAIR, A SNAKE.` → `LEFT SIDE: BRAID, EARRING, ANKLET.` → `ONE FIGURE, SPLIT DOWN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: Brahma, the creator, has a problem. He makes beings from his own mind, and they don't multiply. The world stays small. So he does tapas, and Shiva appears to him in this form, half himself and half the goddess. Brahma bows, and asks the goddess side for help. She gives a power of her own so that creation can go on, and in the story the world begins to grow through women and men together. So the picture isn't a riddle. It's an answer. Creation doesn't go forward on one half. The name says it plainly: ardha, half, nari, woman, ishvara, lord. The lord who is half woman. Some Shaiva teachers put it this way: Shiva and Shakti, the god and his power, are never really two. One poet put it in an image a student could use. At the opening of his long poem the Raghuvamsha, Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined, he says, like a word and its meaning. Try separating those. A word with no meaning is noise. A meaning with no word can't be said. That's the last of our selections from the Shiva Purana, and it gathers up the rest. A pillar of fire no one could measure. Sati, who wouldn't hear her husband mocked. Kama burned by the third eye. Parvati's tapas and the visitor who was Shiva. A wedding where a mother learned to look again. Three cities and one arrow. And now the two who were circling each other through all those stories, standing in one body. Tomorrow, another form Shiva takes: the dancer.
screen: `BRAHMA'S WORLD WON'T GROW.` · `HALF SHIVA, HALF THE GODDESS.` · `LIKE A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` · `THE SELECTIONS, GATHERED UP.` · then, large: `NEITHER HALF WORKS ALONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: two halves, one breath. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring your attention to the right side of the body: the right hand, the right shoulder, the right foot. Breathe there for a few breaths. Then move to the left side: left hand, left shoulder, left foot. Breathe there. Then let the line down the middle go soft, and feel the whole body breathing as one thing. If you pray, you can say the names Shiva and Shakti, or the name of God you use, and let them rest together. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Purana. Today's selection, and the last: Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman, the answer when Brahma's world wouldn't grow.

Your line: the Shiva Purana, in selections. Today, notice one pair in your life that only works together, two hands, two voices, a word and its meaning, and thank both halves. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-four.

screen: `DAY 1124 COUNTS.` → `THE SHIVA PURANA, COMPLETE.` → `TOMORROW: NATARAJA EXPLAINED.`

howItsDone: Ardhanarishvara, Shiva as half man and half woman, appears in temple sculpture and bronzes and is worshiped as a picture of Shiva and Shakti inseparable; Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha opens by bowing to Parvati and Shiva joined like a word and its meaning.

fork.setup: you're Brahma. the beings you make don't multiply, and Shiva has appeared to you as half man, half woman. whom do you ask for help?
options: no one; you try again alone.
fork.reveal: Brahma asks the goddess side, and she gives a power of her own so that creation goes on. one half alone couldn't do it.

original.note: Sanskrit: Ardhanarishvara, from ardha (half), nari (woman) and ishvara (lord): the lord who is half woman.

trapdoor: what you thought: a strange half-and-half statue.
what it means: Shiva and Shakti in one body, the answer when creation wouldn't grow on one half.
what a scholar hears: Kalidasa, Raghuvamsha 1.1, bowing to Parvati and Parameshvara, the world's parents, joined like word and meaning.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Shatarudra Samhita (the Ardhanarishvara form appearing to Brahma)

notes: Last Shiva Purana selection (1118–1124). The summary lists the 1118–1121 writer's selections as written on disk.

Confirm the Shiva Purana, Shatarudra Samhita, as the location of the Ardhanarishvara episode: Brahma's mind-born creation not multiplying, his tapas, Shiva appearing half-woman, Brahma asking the goddess for help. The detail of what power she gives (and her rebirth as Daksha's daughter in some readings) was kept general.

Iconographic details (right side male with matted hair and snake earring; left side female with braid, round earring, breast, anklet) describe common images; side assignment is the usual one but confirm.
Raghuvamsha 1.1 paraphrased: Kalidasa salutes Parvati and Parameshvara, parents of the world, joined like speech (vak) and meaning (artha).
Editor pass: softened the sweeping 'In Shaiva thought, Shiva and Shakti are never really two' to 'Some Shaiva teachers put it this way'.
